Measured against a **completed migration** for the first time, and it changed
the answer.

A finished DeltaV system — 761 modules, built by hand from this same ABB project
— was read back against what the tool proposes from the export. Four things were
wrong, and all four are the kind that only a real answer sheet exposes.

**A tag is not a module.** `proposed_modules.csv` had one row per tagged block,
which sizes the job by an order of magnitude too high. The soft water tank level
is seven ABB tags — the measurement, a second range, the raw end, an alarm, a
latch and two edges — and **one** DeltaV module. A motor is its hour meters and
its run feedback as well; alarm limits (`-HA`, `-HiHi`, `-LA`) are parameters of
the measurement's module and not modules, and not one of the 470 such tags in
the real export exists as a module in the finished system. Rows are now one per
device, with the absorbed tags listed so nothing disappears quietly: 7,343
source tags resolve to 2,583 devices.

**The block types that matter most had no entry.** `IDF_1` is the plant device
block — motors, pumps, solenoid valves — 414 of them, and the legend had never
heard of it, so the tool reported the 414 most important tags in the project as
"unmapped, needs a decision". `C_CU` (126 control loops) and `CT_ANA` (57
totalisers) likewise. Twenty-five block types are now characterised, each
against evidence from the real export, and each labelled `vendor` or `site` so a
block from *this project's* own library is never presented as a fact about
Freelance.

**`FDT12_DEV` was the opposite mistake.** 366 instances, reported as an unmapped
decision, and it is not a plant device at all — it is the diagnostics of an I/O
*card* ("PSP1 Node 2 Card 1"). None of the 366 became a module. They are
`hardware` now, and 366 false work items are gone.

**The class is fitted, not looked up.** The first-match ladder is replaced by
evidence that combines and can disagree: what the block type declares, what the
tag's ISA letters say, the shape of the I/O the device owns, and the engineer's
own words — each able to *abstain*, bounded by a ceiling set by the strongest
kind of evidence behind it, and gated by whether the class can physically hold
the device's I/O (the digits in `V12`, `M11`, `MFR22` are the I/O counts). Every
proposal carries its score, its evidence axis by axis, its runners-up, and any
axis that voted against the winner. Against the finished system, **95 of 99
devices agree** on what the device is.

# v6

**Fixed: listing the registered OPC servers crashed the helper on machines that
have classic OPC installed.**

The helper asked Windows for the OPC server-list object, then used the answer as
if it were a different kind of object and called through it — an access violation
that killed it silently, with no message to show. It only happened where classic
OPC (OPCEnum) is actually registered: everywhere else the request fails first and
the tool correctly reported "no classic OPC here", which is why this went unseen.
It now asks for the interface it intends to use, matching what the rest of the
helper already did.

## v13.6

**Work it out for me pairs what the comparison pairs.** The proposal was built from the raw
top-level names, and the comparison does not match on those: it first expands every composite
definition into one entry per use and looks each one up by *classifier : name*. So the
auto-map was fed dozens of generated composite names (`__62B069D2_5F4D7CF0__`) that no rule
can pair, and it let a phase class pair with a unit class that merely shared a name -- which
is how it proposed `XFR -> A` on a trainee export. It now works from the comparison's own
keys, and a name pairs only with the same name of the same kind.

On TRAINING against TRAINING_A the proposal went from one rule pairing 150 names to a map
pairing 215 of 228 (222 of 228 the other way round); what is left is two classes the trainee
genuinely renamed.

- **Least difference breaks a tie.** Two rules that pair equally many names are decided by
  which one's pairs differ least in parameter content, then by which replacement looks most
  like its find. Without it, `_SETUP_A -> _XFR` -- a swap, same kind, same children -- could
  win over `_SETUP_A -> _SETUP`.
- **Small patterns and single renames.** A suffix carried by only two names (`_XFR`) is
  found on a second, relaxed pass, and a name renamed on its own (`AGITATE -> AGITATE_A`,
  `TRAINING -> TRAINING_A`) gets a whole-name rule.
- **Names the map would break are protected.** `_BA -> _A` also rewrites `_JKT_SEQ_EM_BA`,
  which is the same in both files; an identity rule keeps it paired, and keeps every
  reference to it from reading as a parameter difference.
- The proposal takes well under a second on the training pair (it took up to 30).

## v13.5

**The replication map can be worked out for you.** The editor has a *Work it out for me*
button. With both files parsed it reads the top-level element names on each side, gated by
the template the run will use, and proposes the map: collect candidate fragments, score each
by how many names it actually pairs, keep the best, then look again at what is *still
unpaired* and propose the next. That second pass is what finds an area number renamed

pairs the same names as `_E -> _B` and also rewrites every tag that merely ends in E.

# v7 — Generate with Copilot actually works in the shipped build

v6's button failed with a "permission denied" error naming a file in a temp
folder. The action library it drafts from was packaged into a *folder* of the
same name instead of as a file, so the tool opened the folder — which Windows
reports as a rights problem rather than a missing file, which is why it looked
like one. Nothing was wrong with your machine or your permissions.

Fixed in the packaging and in how the tool locates the library, and the build
spec is now covered by a test, since this was invisible to every test that ran
from source.

# v6 — Draft a command's logic from a description

**New "Generate with Copilot…" button, beside Browse and Build Logic.** Describe what
each command should do — "close all the outlet valves, open the inlet valve, wait for
the tank to reach setpoint" — and the Generate tab drafts the step sequence for you.

**The model never writes DeltaV code.** EMTools already ships 68 hand-written action
templates, and the model's whole job is two choices per action: which template, and
which device. The expressions come out of the library with your device names filled in,
so what you get is text somebody wrote by hand — not generated Structured Text that
merely looks right. An action naming a template or a device this EM does not have is
reported and left out rather than guessed at.

**Nothing is applied without you seeing it.** The draft opens in the same Logic Builder
you would have used to build it by hand, so you can correct any step before saving;
until you press Save in that window, the EM's logic is unchanged. Anything the draft
could not resolve is listed first.

"All the outlet valves" becomes ONE action over the whole family, not six — six
separate actions would each wait on the one before it, so the valves would move in
sequence instead of together.

What it cannot do: logic that BRANCHES on an operator's answer. Every action is a
template instance, so "open whichever valve they picked" has no template to be, and
comes back as a straight list for you to turn into IF/ELSIF in the editor.

## v13

Two new formal checks, and sharper findings on SFC logic and expressions.

- **Alarm flood and rationalization audit.** A new ISA-18.2 / IEC 62682 check flags unsuppressed consequential alarms that can cascade into a flood, chattering risks (zero deadband or no debounce), and incomplete rationalization, and checks the priority distribution against the guideline.
- **SFC timing and watchdog safety.** A new check models each SFC's timing to find step actions that outlast a watchdog, transitions that can confirm before a timeout, and parallel branches that can drift apart.
- **Dead-end steps are proved, not guessed.** The SFC graph check now also runs a formal deadlock test and warns on a step with no viable outgoing path, which would halt the phase.
- **Division hazards in expressions.** Beyond a literal zero, a denominator that evaluates to zero, or whose range crosses zero, is now reported as a formal hazard.
- **Fewer false unresolved library references.** The graphics check now also finds library references stored under CLASS_ prefixed or trailing-underscore file names.
- **Its own icon on the taskbar.** The window now registers its own Windows taskbar identity and puts its icon on the top-level window, so the tool groups under its own name and shows its own icon instead of a generic one.

**The batch course's instructor read a real run and sent back three findings that
were the tool's, not the trainee's.** All three are fixed.

- **A branching logic ends where it ends.** AGITATE's run logic stops at MONITOR
  on the timed path and COMPLETE on the other; grading every end against one name
  reported the phase twice for being right ("[STD-6] Last step is 'MONITOR',
  expected 'COMPLETE'" and "[STD-12] Last step 'MONITOR' does not set \"Run Logic
  Complete\""). A logic passes when one of its ends is the step the standard names,
  and only that end is graded on its message. A logic whose ends are all something

# v6 (not yet built)
**`patina carchive` — read an undocumented MFC file format out of the binary
that writes it.** Aimed at the case where the binary is not the artefact you
care about: a proprietary document format with no schema.

- **The `CRuntimeClass` table** with each class's `sizeof`, its **archive
  schema**, and its base. The schema is the fact that matters and Patina was
  discarding it: a class whose schema is `0xFFFF` is `DECLARE_DYNAMIC`, so
  `CArchive` **never announces it by name** — a reader that expects every class
  to be tagged will mis-frame every record after the first.
- **The inlined `CArchive` fixed-width accessors**, with each one's **field
  width** and direction. Direction is decided by which side of the `mov` the
  archive buffer is on, not by anything sitting near it.

Validated against an independently hand-derived model of `GraphicsEd.dll`
(FactoryTalk View's graphics editor): 360 classes, and every checkable fact
agrees — `ZText` 504 bytes deriving from `ZUnrotatedRect`, `ZButtonElement` 3480
deriving from `ZPolygon`, the three `ZConnection*` classes alone at schema 1,

`Serialize` at `0x6244ff90`. Generalises: RSLinx gives 198 classes and 4
primitives; a non-MFC binary reports nothing.

# v5
Historian export comparator -- new `compare` CLI verb, no DeltaV connection needed

DvHistExport is no longer connection-only. `app.py` is now the built entry point
(`build.ps1`'s `-Entry "app"`): a `compare` verb on the command line runs headless,
before Tk or pythonnet/the DeltaV DLLs are even imported. No verb still opens the
window exactly as before, and `--selftest` is unchanged.

`DvHistExport.exe compare SOURCE.csv TARGET.csv --out REPORT.xlsx` compares two
historian exports (e.g. this tool's own "Export CSV..." output against a PI or
dataPARC export) for value/quality/timestamp agreement, matching samples within a
configurable time tolerance rather than requiring identical timestamps. It samples
`ceil(sqrt(N)) + 1` tags out of the total configured -- the same formula a real
Cornerstone dataPARC IQ/OQ deliverable uses to verify ongoing collection by hand
(72 of a 5000-tag system) -- chosen by even stride across the sorted tag list so
the sample is reproducible from the tag list alone. Writes a Sample Selection /
Comparison Evidence / Summary workbook. The comparison engine (`shared.histcompare`)
is shared with FHXport's new `historian-compare` verb, since neither side of a
historian-to-historian comparison is DeltaV-specific.

Also: the window now registers its own Windows taskbar identity (AppUserModelID), so it groups and shows its own icon on the taskbar instead of a generic one.

# v4
The quality column was inverted — every good sample was flagged bad

The sample list tested `status != 0` to decide whether to highlight a row. Quality
lives in the top two bits of the DeltaV status byte, so a good sample is 0x80–0xFF
and only 0x00 passed that test. The result was backwards: every GOODCASCADE and
GOODNONCASCADE sample was highlighted as bad, and the one genuinely bad byte
(0x00, BAD/non-specific) was shown as fine.

The status byte is now decoded through `shared.deltav.status` rather than guessed
at. Samples carry readable Quality, Substatus and Limit, the list highlights only
what is actually not-good, and the read summary says how many samples were not
good. The CSV export gains `quality`, `substatus`, `limit` and `is_good` columns
alongside the raw bytes, which are unchanged.

`archive_status` (holes, manual edits) is still exported raw — those flag
meanings are not yet documented.

# v27

A rebuild; the tool itself behaves as described under v25.

- **No new behaviour in this release.** The pattern warnings, the "0 matches" explanations and the write-time checks described under v25 are all in this build.

# v25

- **Replacing a whole expression now works.** Collapsing an expression onto a single tag, re-shaping one
  (dropping some terms and adding others), and changing an `and` to an `or` where that changes the order the
  picture evaluates in — none of these could ever be written. Each was routed to an engine that built the
  edit, and a check at the very end refused it; because that check refuses the WHOLE picture, one awkward
  expression meant nothing in the file was written. Measured before: 0 of 8. Now every one of them applies,
  and the finished file is re-read to prove it.
  - The message you would have seen was *"N expression(s) would ship unreadable"* or *"N expression(s) would
    ship with N missing data-source connection(s)"*.
  - **No picture was ever damaged by this.** The refusal happened before anything was written. If a colleague
    ran Picture Repair on the file and it came back healthy, that was correct — the file was never the
    problem, the edit was. Both messages now say so.
  - Where a replacement needs a longer tag name than the picture has room for in that slot, that ONE
    expression is reported skipped with the reason, and the rest of the file is written as normal.
- **A new check that reads the finished picture before writing it.** Every earlier check inspected the edit
  in memory, and that is not the same thing as the file. An edit can look perfect in memory and still write a
  picture where fifteen expressions have operands with nothing driving them — the failure where an alarm
  colour reads correctly in the editor and simply never changes on screen. Every write is now re-read and its
  live-data connections compared against the original; if the edit made them worse, nothing is written.
- **"0 matches" now tells you WHY.** A pattern that finds nothing used to look identical whether
  the text is genuinely absent or the pattern is one clause away from right. The preview now
  works out how far the pattern DOES match and names the clause the picture stops agreeing with,
  with an example of the closest value it found. A 640-character alarm-colour pattern that
  reported nothing turned out to end in a `_CND_01/DEPRIORITIZE` clause that particular picture
  does not have — visible immediately now, where before it meant dumping every expression in the
  file by hand.
- **A replacement that DELETES tags now says which ones.** This is the quiet one. A greedy `(.*)`
  in the Find swallows whatever sits between the tokens you wrote, and if the replacement only
  writes `${1}` back, everything the wildcard ate is deleted. The rule looks like a rename and
  the preview row is 600 characters wide, so two alarm terms vanishing from the middle are
  invisible. Every preview row for an expression now names the tag references the rewrite would
  remove — whether it is applied or skipped.
  - Real case: a pattern naming `_TE_01`, `_TE_01B` and `_ZS_01` matched rooms that also read
    `_HT_01`, `_HT_01B` and `_ZS_02`, and would have dropped four of the five alarms each room
    monitors.
- **Removing a term from an expression now works.** It routed to the right engine and built the right token
  graph, but the shortened display string was moved in the process and the expression was left with no
  display text at all — so the whole-picture check refused the file. Every attempt to delete a term was
  refused; measured 0 of 6 before, 6 of 6 now. The display is rewritten in place, which is what the
  rename path has always done — both now share the one implementation.
- **The command-line tool now shows the same warnings as the GUI.** `operate-cli fr --regex`
  printed none of them: greedy wildcards, capture groups the replacement never reads, the
  `$1_TE_01` group-name trap, over-wide

# v6
It asks DeltaV what is waiting, instead of guessing

Scanning the network used to say nothing at all about decommissioned nodes.
That was not a subtle failure: the probe built its list of addresses from the
device table, and a node with no identity is at none of them, so it swept
twenty-two addresses the node could not be at and never looked at the one place
it was. The single question most people open this tool to ask went unanswered.

**It now reads the list out of DeltaV itself.** DeltaV keeps Decommissioned

one DvScan can call - the same one DeltaV Diagnostics uses to draw that view.
So the answer is exact rather than inferred: a row per node, with no packet
capture and no Administrator. On the system this was built against it returned
twenty-two nodes, including two that had spent two days refusing to appear
anywhere else.

Where that call is unavailable it falls back to probing the default address,
and is careful about what that proves. Every unassigned node answers on the
same address, so a probe can say **at least one** node is waiting and cannot
say how many. It says "at least one" rather than inventing a count.

presenting a button that quietly does nothing.
